pattern: Myth vs fact debunk (remade from the 'Just let them cry it out' separation anxiety myth-buster and the 'alone time is trained, not forced' format)
why: Opening on a common bad tip creates instant tension, and each myth-fact pair gives the anxious first-time owner a reason to keep swiping to the calm, doable answer.

slides.headline: Your dog cries the second you leave?
body: You're not a bad owner. Swipe for what helps.

slides.headline: Myth: just let them cry it out
body: It's everywhere online, but pushing past their limit
can make being home alone feel scarier.

slides.headline: Fact: calm alone time is a skill
body: Practised in tiny steps your dog can cope with.
Hound builds a plan for your dog's age and problem.

slides.headline: Myth: you need hours of training every day
body: Fact: one short exercise a day, about 10 minutes.
Small, regular practice is what adds up.

slides.headline: Myth: only practise when you actually need to leave
body: Fact: short, easy absences on a calm day build confidence.
Track the small wins with progress and streaks.

caption: Leaving the house shouldn't come with a side of guilt. Calm alone time is practised in small steps, not forced. Take the age quiz at houndapp.xyz for a plan built for your dog.

findings.message: The post targets separation anxiety (crying when left, #separationanxiety) but never suggests a vet or qualified behaviorist for severe cases; add a short line such as 'For severe separation anxiety, talk to your vet or a qualified behaviourist' on a slide or in the caption.
findings.excerpt: Your dog cries the second you leave?

findings.message: Five slides use AI-generated photoreal images of people and dogs, so apply the platform's AI-generated content label (TikTok or Meta) at posting time per the pack checklist.
findings.excerpt: image: generated prompt: Candid iPhone photo

slides.issues: Strong, relatable opener: the dog looking up at the owner at the door tells the story without words. The bottom gradient keeps the headline crisp. The 'cries' accent colour works. Lighting is a touch polished and staged, but there are no obvious AI tells. The subline is small but readable.

Very native, phone-camera feel, and the dejected dog by the door matches the myth. Text sits on a plain grey wall, so it is clean. Body copy is on the small side for phone viewing. The top of the frame is mostly empty wall, so there is room to bump up the body size.

Real product is clearly visible: the app quiz screen on a phone, which clears the gate. The floating phone over a heavily blurred background reads as a brand ad rather than a creator post. In-app copy uses US 'behavior' while the carousel is UK English. The bottom of the phone is cropped close to the edge. Consider a hand holding the phone in a real home setting for more native feel.

Natural, warm training moment with a believable dog and hands. The body copy runs over a bright window and cabinet area on the right, so 'adds up' and '10 minutes' lose contrast. A stronger top scrim or text shadow is needed. 'Fact' is buried in the body while it is a headline on slide 3, which makes the format inconsistent.

The dog, which is the point of the scene (calm while the owner leaves), sits bottom right and is almost fully hidden under the headline and gradient. The scene reads as just a woman leaving. The headline is long, at three lines, and the body wraps awkwardly ('confidence.' orphaned). Also, the 'streaks' claim is not shown.

final.notes: Gate passes: the real app quiz screen is visible on slide 3, and houndapp.xyz is the CTA on slide 6. Narrative flow from hook to myth/fact to quiz is solid and empathetic. Biggest fixes: (1) reshoot slide 5 so the calm dog is visible above the text; (2) add contrast behind slide 4 body copy; (3) make the myth/fact format consistent across slides; (4) fix the US 'behavior' spelling in the app screen for a UK audience; (5) lighten the slide 6 overlay. Slide 3 would feel more native as a hand-held phone shot in a real room.

slides.issues: Strong, relatable scene: a beagle staring up at an owner at the door, with a warm natural hallway. The headline sits on a clean dark gradient and reads well, and the orange 'cries' accent works. The subline is small at phone size, so bump it 10 to 15 percent. The image is slightly too polished and staged, which nudges it towards stock. The hook is good but generic: adding a specific detail such as 'howls for 20 minutes' would sharpen it.

The image is mostly an empty sofa and a plant. The dog is pushed to the bottom edge and partly cropped, so the emotional subject of 'cry it out' is barely there. The body copy sits over busy monstera leaves and relies on a drop shadow, which gets noisy at phone size. Overall it reads like an interiors photo rather than a dog-anxiety post.

As a mid-carousel slide, its swipe pull is moderate.

The headline is the longest in the set at three lines, and the body breaks badly with 'confidence.' orphaned. The woman smiling back at the camera feels posed. Shorten the headline and move the text up, or use a frame where the dog sits mid-frame with clear floor space below.
